content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 4: Security Lab Setup and Tools. It builds practical understanding of Command-Line and Network Utilities with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Command-Line and Network Utilities helps you observe a real boundary instead of assuming that browser, proxy, transport, and server behavior are interchangeable. Use maintained cryptographic libraries and approved configurations; keep keys and secrets out of source code and logs, scope access, and define rotation and recovery.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Command-Line and Network Utilities can be understood through this sequence: Receive untrusted data → Keep data separate → Validate safe interface → Regression test. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 26.1 Using HTTP clients for authorized testing; 26.2 Inspecting HTTP headers and response codes; 26.3 DNS and connectivity diagnostics; 26.4 TLS certificate inspection; 26.5 Capturing reproducible test results. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Use maintained cryptographic libraries and approved configurations; keep keys and secrets out of source code and logs, scope access, and define rotation and recovery. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.
